newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian busmaker NABI to list shares in Budapest.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian busmaker NABI to list shares in Budapest.

text.p: The First Hungary Fund (FHF) said on Friday its Hungarian busmaker subsidiary North American Bus Industries Kft (NABI) started on Friday seeking investors for an initial public offering of 1,704,700 new shares.

Subsequently, FHF will offer 65,300 of its existing NABI shares in a public offering to Hungarian institutional investors, and NABI will seek to list its shares in category B of the Budapest Stock Exchange, the fund said in a statement.

NABI -- which assembles buses in Alabama from Hungarian-built bodies and chassis mainly for the U.S. market -- will offer the new shares to institutional investors in Hungary and other places outside the United States, the statement said.
"The shares will be marketed to investors in the institutional offering on... a price range of 2,850 to 3,280 forints, valuing the company at 12.7 to 14.7 billion forints," the statement said.
The busmaker started on Friday promoting the sale in "selected European cities, commencing in Budapest," the statement added.
NABI had net income of $1.3 million on net sales of $23.2 million on a consolidated basis for the three months of 1997, the statement said.

"We expect NABI to have a full-year net income of $5.3 million on net sales revenue close to $120 million on a consolidated basis (in 1997)," Csaba Zoltan, a FHF senior investment manager and a NABI board member, told Reuters.
The company reported a net income of $3.1 million on net sales revenue of $77.8 million in 1996, FHF's statement said.

FHF -- a closed-end equity fund based in Jersey, Channel Islands -- recently became NABI's sole owner by buying 25 percent of the busmaker's shares held by Hungarian state-owned busmaker Ikarus Jarmugyarto Rt.
NABI, which competes in the U.S. market for 40-foot and 60-foot heavy duty transit buses operated by municipalities, sold 302 buses in an estimated market of 3,000 units in 1996, Zoltan said.
The busmaker, whose assets totalled $40.6 million at the end of 1996, expects to boost its market share in 1997 by increasing sales to over 400 units amid a stagnating market, he said.
"We do not expect significant growth in the market," Zoltan said.
